newsitem.title: USA: D.C. panel says rejects Clinton District plan.
newsitem.headline: D.C. panel says rejects Clinton District plan.

text.p: District of Columbia's 12-member city council agreed Tuesday to reject President Clinton's proposed financial revitalization plan for D.C. because it would cut a $660 million payment-in-lieu-of-taxes that the city gets annually from Capitol Hill.
The council unanimously signed a draft resolution on the issue introduced by D.C. councilmen Harold Brazil and Frank Smith, according to Brazil aides.

The resolution says that the council will not sign any upcoming memorandum of understanding with the U.S. government and the city's financial control board on federal relief for the city if the $660 million is eliminated.

The document says that when Congress voted in 1991 to reimburse the city annually for the federal government's use of D.C. property, that federal payment was never intended to cover the city costs for Medicaid, roads, infrastructure, prisons and state courts, the council said.
The $3.9 billion, five-year revitalization plan proposed by the White House on January 14 would make the federal government largely responsible for those costs.
But it would save the city only about $770 million over the five years because it would require the city to forfeit the annual $660 million payment.

Brazil said any agreement to wipe out the federal payment "constitutes unsound public and financial policy." He said the President apparently did not get "adequate" advice from Office of Management and Budget chief Frank Raines, who wrote the administration's plan.
The D.C. council will take a formal vote on the resolution shortly, a Brazil aide said.

Meanwhile, four House and Senate subcommittees will hold a joint hearing on March 11 to discuss D.C.'s financial problems and to hear from officials of other U.S. cities that have overcome financial difficulty, a congressional spokesman said.
Host panels are the D.C. subcommittees of the House and Senate Appropriations Committees and of the House Government Reform and Oversight Committee and the Senate Government Affairs Committee.
